questions.q: Gautam picks a counting number, divides it by 1000 and says the answer on his calculator is 0.4567. Show that this cannot be right, and write a division by 10, 100, 1000 or 10000 of a counting number that really does give 0.4567.
questions.a: A counting number has no digits after the point. Dividing by 1000 moves the point 3 places left, so the answer can have at most 3 digits after the point, but 0.4567 has 4 (the last digit, 7, is not zero). In other words, 0.4567 × 1000 = 456.7, which is not a counting number. The division that works is 4567 ÷ 10000 = 0.4567.
s: states that dividing a counting number by 1000 gives at most 3 digits after the point
points out 0.4567 has 4 digits after the point, or that 0.4567 × 1000 = 456.7 is not a counting number

questions.q: In an agriculture lab, 10000 mustard seeds together weigh 21.1 g. Given 1 g = 1000 mg, one seed weighs

Students are building a model of a dam for their science fair. The real wall is 28.5 m high and the model is 100 times smaller. A drawing on their chart is 10 times smaller than the model.
(a) Find the height of the wall in the model, in metres and in centimetres.
(b) Find its height in the drawing, in metres and in centimetres.
(c) How many times smaller is the drawing than the real wall? Explain using the movement of the decimal point.
(d) The real wall is 63 m long. How long is it in the drawing, in centimetres?
(e) A gate in the drawing is 4.05 cm wide. Find its real width in metres. (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 28.5 ÷ 100 = 0.285 m = 28.5 cm. (b) 0.285 ÷ 10 = 0.0285 m = 2.85 cm. (c) 1000 times: the point moved 2 places left and then 1 more, 3 places in all, which is a division by 1000 (100 × 10 = 1000). (d) 63 ÷ 1000 = 0.063 m = 6.3 cm. (e) 4.05 × 1000 = 4050 cm = 40.5 m.
s: (a) finds 0.285 m and 28.5 cm
(b) finds 0.0285 m and 2.85 cm
(c) says 1000 times, with 2 + 1 = 3 places moved
(d) finds 6.3 cm
(e) multiplies by 1000 and converts to 40.5 m

questions.q: True or False: Dividing 62.5 by 100 and then by 10 gives the same result as dividing it by 10 and then by 100, and that result is 0.0625. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. 62.5 ÷ 100 = 0.625 and 0.625 ÷ 10 = 0.0625; 62.5 ÷ 10 = 6.25 and 6.25 ÷ 100 = 0.0625. Either way the point moves 3 places left in all.
s: states True
shows both orders give 0.0625, or that the point moves 3 places left either way

questions.q:
A lab balance reading has 3 ones, no tenths, 4 hundredths, 6 thousandths and 2 ten-thousandths.
(a) Write the reading as a decimal and as one fraction with denominator 10000.
(b) Which is the smallest of 10, 100, 1000, 10000 that turns the reading into a counting number when multiplied? Explain.
(c) A further 0.0538 g is placed on the pan. Find the new reading, and the smallest of 10, 100, 1000, 10000 that turns it into a counting number. Why is it not the same multiplier as in (b)? (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 3.0462 = 30462/10000. (b) 10000: the reading has 4 digits after the point, so the point must move 4 places right; multiplying by 1000 gives only 3046.2. (c) 3.0462 + 0.0538 = 3.1000 = 3.1, and 3.1 × 10 = 31, so 10 is enough. The new reading has only zeroes after the tenths place, so only 1 place after the point really counts. Reject 10000 for (c) given only because the first reading needed it.
s: (a) writes 3.0462 (0 in the tenths place) and 30462/10000
(b) chooses 10000 and explains using the 4 digits after the point
(c) finds 3.1 and chooses 10, saying the hundredths, thousandths and ten-thousandths digits are now 0

questions.q:
A postage stamp is 2.6 cm long and 1.5 cm wide.
(a) Find its area in square centimetres by multiplying the decimals.
(b) Ravi measures the same stamp in millimetres, 26 mm by 15 mm, and gets 390 square mm. Given 1 square cm = 100 square mm, show that his answer agrees with (a), and say what this tells you about the number of decimal places in (a). (1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 26 × 15 = 390, and there are 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places, so 2.6 × 1.5 = 3.90 = 3.9 square cm. (b) 390 ÷ 100 = 3.9 square cm, the same. Each cm is 10 mm, so 1 square cm holds 10 × 10 = 100 square mm: one decimal place in each length gives hundredths of a square cm, which is why the product has 2 decimal places before the final zero is dropped.
s: (a) finds 3.9 square cm (or 3.90) with 2 decimal places from 1 + 1
(b) converts 390 square mm to 3.9 square cm and links the 2 decimal places to 10 × 10 = 100

questions.q:
A bill was worked out as 6 × 12.75 + 2.5 × 40, in rupees.
(a) Write a shopping situation that this expression fits, saying what each number stands for.
(b) Find the value of the bill.
(c) How much change is left from ₹200? (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) Any fitting story, for example: 6 pens at ₹12.75 each and 2.5 kg of onions at ₹40 per kg (or 12.75 kg of rice at ₹6 per kg and 2.5 kg of onions at ₹40 per kg). Accept any situation in which each product is a quantity times a rate with units. Reject a story that gives no units, or in which 6 × 12.75 or 2.5 × 40 is not a quantity times a rate (for example, adding the numbers). (b) 6 × 12.75 = 76.5 and 2.5 × 40 = 100, so the bill is ₹176.50. (c) 200 - 176.5 = ₹23.50.
s: (a) writes a situation, with units, in which each product in the expression is a sensible quantity × rate
(b) finds ₹176.50
(c) finds ₹23.50 change

questions.q:
Match each product in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. 12 × 5 tenths  2. 12 × 5 hundredths  3. 5 × 12 thousandths  4. 12 hundredths × 5 hundredths
Column II: a. 0.06  b. 6  c. 0.006  d. 0.6
questions.a: 1-b, 2-d, 3-a, 4-c: 60 tenths = 6, 60 hundredths = 0.6, 60 thousandths = 0.06, and 0.12 × 0.05 = 60 ten-thousandths = 0.006.

questions.q:
Tina goes to her coaching class by auto-rickshaw, 6.8 km each way. The minimum fare is ₹30 and covers the first 1.5 km of a trip; every further kilometre costs ₹14.50. The auto stand also offers a monthly plan: a fixed ₹650 a month, and then only ₹4.25 for each kilometre after the first 1.5 km of a trip. The ₹650 also pays the minimum fare for the first 1.5 km of every trip, so no ₹30 is charged on the plan.
(a) Find the ordinary fare for one trip.
(b) In a month she makes 8 trips. Find the cost of 8 trips at the ordinary fare and on the monthly plan, and say which is cheaper and by how much.
(c) In a month with exam leave she makes only 6 trips. Compare the two costs, and advise her how to decide each month. (1 + 2 + 2)
questions.a: (a) 6.8 - 1.5 = 5.3 km beyond the minimum; 5.3 × 14.5 = 76.85; fare = 30 + 76.85 = ₹106.85. (b) Ordinary: 8 × 106.85 = ₹854.80. Plan: 8 × 5.3 = 42.4 km; 42.4 × 4.25 = 180.20; cost = 650 + 180.20 = ₹830.20. The plan is cheaper by 854.80 - 830.20 = ₹24.60. (c) Ordinary: 6 × 106.85 = ₹641.10. Plan: 6 × 5.3 = 31.8 km, 31.8 × 4.25 = 135.15, and 650 + 135.15 = ₹785.15, so the ordinary fare saves ₹144.05. (Even for 7 trips the ordinary fare, ₹747.95, is less than the plan, about ₹807.68.) Advice: take the plan only in a month with 8 or more trips; otherwise pay the ordinary fare. Accept advice that rests on comparing the two costs for the number of trips expected (such as "work out both costs for that month's trips and pick the smaller"). Reject advice that does not use the costs found, such as "always take the plan".
s: (a) finds 5.3 km and the fare ₹106.85
(b) finds ₹854.80 for the ordinary fare and 42.4 km, ₹830.20 on the plan
(b) says the plan is cheaper by ₹24.60
(c) finds ₹641.10 and ₹785.15 and says the ordinary fare is cheaper for 6 trips
(c) advises by the number of trips in the month (plan only for about 8 or more trips), tied to the costs found

questions.q: Ayaan finds 3.06 × 0.24. He works out 306 × 24 = 7344, counts 2 + 2 = 4 decimal places and writes 0.7344. Dia says the answer has to be 7.344, because 3.06 is more than 3 and "the product cannot be smaller than 1 when one number is more than 3". Who is right? Check by using fractions, and find where the other person's reasoning fails.
questions.a: Ayaan is right. 3.06 × 0.24 = 306/100 × 24/100 = 7344/10000 = 0.7344. Dia's reasoning fails because 0.24 is less than 1, so the product is smaller than 3.06; it is only about a quarter of 3.06 and can be below 1.
s: concludes Ayaan is right and the product is 0.7344
explains that multiplying by 0.24, which is less than 1, makes 3.06 smaller, so Dia's reason fails

questions.q:
A photocopier multiplies every length by the zoom number that is set on it. Fatima's drawing is 12.4 cm wide. She enlarges it at zoom 1.5, then copies the copy at zoom 0.5, expecting to get her original size back.
(a) Find the width after each copy.
(b) Is the final copy wider or narrower than the original? Which one zoom number would give the final copy in a single step? Check it on 12.4.
(c) Among 0.5, 0.6, 0.75 and 0.8, which zoom undoes an enlargement at zoom 1.25? Show it by multiplying.
(d) Without working on the width, say whether copying at zoom 1.1 and then at zoom 0.9 gives a copy wider or narrower than the original, with a reason.
(e) Find the width of Fatima's drawing after those two copies in (d). (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 12.4 × 1.5 = 18.6 cm, then 18.6 × 0.5 = 9.3 cm. (b) Narrower. 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75, and 12.4 × 0.75 = 9.3 cm, the same as the two steps. (c) 0.8, because 1.25 × 0.8 = 1, so the length comes back unchanged. (d) Narrower: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, which is between 0 and 1, so it makes the length smaller. (e) 12.4 × 0.99 = 12.276 cm. In (d), accept any reason that uses 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99 being less than 1; reject "the same size, because 0.1 is added and then taken away".
s: (a) finds 18.6 cm and 9.3 cm
(b) says narrower and shows the single zoom 0.75 gives 9.3 cm
(c) chooses 0.8 with 1.25 × 0.8 = 1
(d) says narrower because 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99 is less than 1
(e) finds 12.276 cm

questions.q: Sita thinks of a decimal k greater than 0. She finds that k × 3.2 is less than 3.2 but greater than k. What must be true of k?
questions.a: k lies between 0 and 1: the product is less than 3.2 only when the other number is less than 1, and then it lies between the two numbers. If k = 1 the product equals 3.2, and if k is greater than 1 the product is more than 3.2.

questions.q:
A rubber ball is dropped from a height of 2.5 m. After each bounce it rises to 0.6 times the height it fell from.
(a) Find the height it rises to after the 1st, 2nd and 3rd bounces.
(b) After which bounce does it first rise to less than 0.5 m? Show the height.
(c) Kiran says, "If it keeps bouncing like this, the height will become 0 one day." Is she right if each bounce really multiplies the height by 0.6? Give a reason using what multiplying by 0.6 does. (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 2.5 × 0.6 = 1.5 m, 1.5 × 0.6 = 0.9 m, 0.9 × 0.6 = 0.54 m. (b) After the 4th bounce: 0.54 × 0.6 = 0.324 m, which is less than 0.5 m (0.54 m after the 3rd is not). (c) No. Multiplying by 0.6, a number between 0 and 1, makes the height smaller each time, but 0.6 of a height that is more than 0 is still more than 0 (0.6 × 0.324 = 0.1944, and so on), so by this rule the height never becomes 0. Accept "it gets smaller and smaller but never reaches 0". Reject "yes", or "no" with no reason.
s: (a) finds 1.5 m, 0.9 m and 0.54 m
(b) says the 4th bounce, with 0.324 m
(c) says no: multiplying by 0.6 makes the height smaller but a part of a positive height is never 0

questions.q: True or False: Given 37 × 43 = 1591, the two products 3.7 × 4.3 and 0.37 × 43 are equal, even though their factors are different. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. 3.7 × 4.3 has 1 + 1 = 2 decimal places and 0.37 × 43 has 2 + 0 = 2 decimal places, so both are 15.91.
s: states True
shows both products have 2 decimal places and equal 15.91

questions.q: Using each of the digits 2, 3, 7 and 8 once, Meher fills the boxes □.□ × □.□. She puts the two largest digits in the ones places and tries 8.3 × 7.2. She says, "The larger tenths digit should go with the larger ones digit, so this is the greatest product possible." Test her claim against 8.2 × 7.3 and give your verdict.
questions.a: Her claim is wrong, although her first idea of using 8 and 7 in the ones places is sound. 8.3 × 7.2 = 59.76 and 8.2 × 7.3 = 59.86, so 8.2 × 7.3 is greater by 0.10. The larger tenths digit should go with the smaller ones digit.
s: concludes her claim is wrong because 59.86 is greater

questions.q:
The running track of a park is a regular 8-sided shape, and one lap is 30.6 m. A second track, a regular 6-sided shape, has the same lap length.
(a) Find the side of the 8-sided track.
(b) Find the side of the 6-sided track.
(c) How many centimetres longer is a side of the 6-sided track? (1 + 1 + 1)
s: (a) finds 3.825 m
(b) finds 5.1 m
(c) finds 1.275 m and converts it to 127.5 cm

questions.q: Hema shares 261 m of rope equally among 8 teams, dividing by place value. She has reached 32 in the quotient, with 5 Ones left, and has just shared out the Tenths. What is left now, and what must she turn it into for the next step?
questions.a: 2 Tenths, regrouped as 20 Hundredths: 5 Ones = 50 Tenths, each team gets 6 Tenths (48 Tenths), so 2 Tenths are left, and these become 20 Hundredths. Going on, each team gets 2 Hundredths, then 5 Thousandths, so 261 ÷ 8 = 32.625.

questions.q:
Rupa divides counting numbers by first making the denominator 10, 100, 1000 or 10000.
(a) By what number should she multiply the numerator and the denominator of 347/40 and of 347/125? Write both as decimals this way.
(b) Find the multiplier for 347/16 and write it as a decimal this way.
(c) Check (b) by long division, saying at which step the decimal point enters the quotient, and say which method you would choose for 347/16, with a reason. (2 + 1 + 2)
questions.a: (a) 25 (40 × 25 = 1000), so 347/40 = 8675/1000 = 8.675; and 8 (125 × 8 = 1000), so 347/125 = 2776/1000 = 2.776. (b) 625 (16 × 625 = 10000), so 347/16 = 216875/10000 = 21.6875. (c) 347 ÷ 16: 21 Ones and 11 Ones remain; regrouping them as 110 Tenths is when the point enters; then 6 Tenths with 14 remaining, 8 Hundredths with 12 remaining, 7 Thousandths with 8 remaining, 5 Ten-thousandths with 0 remaining, giving 21.6875, the same. Either choice is accepted with a reason tied to these numbers: for example, long division, because 625 is not an easy multiplier to spot, or the fraction method, because it needs only one multiplication. A choice with no reason, or a reason not tied to the numbers ("it is easier"), does not earn the mark.
s: (a) gives 25 and 8.675
(a) gives 8 and 2.776
(b) gives 625 and 21.6875
(c) confirms 21.6875 by long division, placing the point when 11 Ones become 110 Tenths
(c) chooses a method with a reason tied to these numbers

questions.q: Tara finds 12.18 ÷ 6 and writes 2.3. She explains, "12 Ones gives 2, and 18 ÷ 6 gives 3." Test her answer by multiplying, find the exact step of her mistake, and give the correct quotient.
questions.a: 2.3 × 6 = 13.8, not 12.18, so she is wrong. After 12 Ones ÷ 6 = 2, the next place holds 1 Tenth, which cannot be shared among 6, so the quotient needs 0 Tenths. Regrouping gives 18 Hundredths, and 18 ÷ 6 = 3 Hundredths. So 12.18 ÷ 6 = 2.03.
s: multiplies 2.3 × 6 = 13.8 and says it does not give 12.18
identifies that 1 Tenth cannot be shared, so a 0 goes in the Tenths place
gives 2.03

questions.q:
At a school fête, 5 litres of nimbu pani is poured equally into 8 jugs.
(a) Using an equivalent fraction with denominator 1000, find how many millilitres go in one jug.
(b) How many litres are in 3 such jugs? (1 + 1)
s: (a) writes 625/1000 and gives 625 mL
(b) finds 1.875 litres

questions.q:
In the style of a problem from Sridharacharya's Patiganita: 7 1/2 is divided by 1 1/4.
(a) Write both mixed numbers as decimals.
(b) Find the quotient by first making the divisor a counting number. (1 + 1)
s: (a) writes 7.5 and 1.25
(b) rewrites as 750 ÷ 125 and finds 6

questions.q: Nitya says, "Dividing by 0.5 is the same as multiplying by 2, dividing by 0.4 is the same as multiplying by 2.5, and dividing by 0.3 is the same as multiplying by 3." Test each part on 18.6, by first turning the divisor into a fraction, and say how far she is right.
questions.a: She is partly right: the first two are right and the third is wrong. 18.6 ÷ 0.5 = 18.6 × 10/5 = 37.2 = 18.6 × 2. 18.6 ÷ 0.4 = 18.6 × 10/4 = 46.5 = 18.6 × 2.5. But 18.6 ÷ 0.3 = 18.6 × 10/3 = 62, while 18.6 × 3 = 55.8. Dividing by 0.3 is multiplying by 10/3, and 10 ÷ 3 = 3.333... never ends, so no short decimal does the job. Accept the verdict only with all three tests shown; reject "she is right" or "she is wrong" with no test.
s: concludes she is partly right, explaining that dividing by 0.3 is multiplying by 10/3, not by 3

questions.q:
Ishan and his sister Pihu walk 540 m from their gate to school. One stride of Ishan's is 0.72 m and one of Pihu's is 0.6 m. Ishan takes 100 strides a minute and Pihu takes 125. They leave together.
(a) Find the number of strides each of them needs, showing how you make each divisor a counting number, and explain why both quotients are greater than 540.
(b) Find the time each takes, and who reaches first and by how many seconds.
(c) Ishan says, "A longer stride always gets you there first." Judge this, using the metres each covers in a minute. (2 + 2 + 1)
questions.a: (a) Ishan: 540 ÷ 0.72 = 54000 ÷ 72 = 750 strides. Pihu: 540 ÷ 0.6 = 5400 ÷ 6 = 900 strides. Both divisors are less than 1, so the quotient is greater than the dividend. (b) Ishan: 750 ÷ 100 = 7.5 minutes. Pihu: 900 ÷ 125 = 7.2 minutes. Pihu reaches first, by 0.3 minute = 18 seconds. (c) His claim is not always true. In a minute Ishan covers 0.72 × 100 = 72 m and Pihu covers 0.6 × 125 = 75 m. His stride is longer, but she takes more strides each minute, and it is the product of the two that decides. Accept a judgement that uses 72 m and 75 m a minute; reject one based on stride length alone.
s: (a) finds 750 strides (54000 ÷ 72) and 900 strides (5400 ÷ 6)
(a) explains that a divisor below 1 gives a quotient above the dividend
(b) finds 7.5 minutes and 7.2 minutes
(b) says Pihu by 18 seconds
(c) finds 72 m and 75 m a minute and rejects the claim

questions.q:
Consider the following statements, to be judged without long division.
Statement 1: 6.4 ÷ 16 is greater than 6.4.
Statement 2: 64 ÷ 0.8 is greater than 64.
Statement 3: 0.64 ÷ 0.8 is greater than 0.64.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. In statements 2 and 3 the divisor 0.8 is less than 1, so the quotient is greater than the dividend (80 and 0.8). In statement 1 the divisor 16 is greater than 1, so the quotient 0.4 is less than the dividend.

questions.q:
A 24 km charity walk will have water tables at equal gaps along the route. The organisers try gaps of 0.8 km, 0.6 km, 0.4 km and 0.2 km. Aman says, "Each time the gap is made 0.2 km shorter, we get the same number of extra gaps."
(a) Find the number of gaps for each choice, showing how you make the divisor a counting number for one of them.
(b) Use your answers to test Aman's claim.
(c) What happens to the number of gaps as the gap gets closer to 0? (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 24 ÷ 0.8 = 240 ÷ 8 = 30; 24 ÷ 0.6 = 240 ÷ 6 = 40; 24 ÷ 0.4 = 240 ÷ 4 = 60; 24 ÷ 0.2 = 240 ÷ 2 = 120. (b) Aman is wrong: the extra gaps are 10, then 20, then 60, not the same each time. (c) The smaller the divisor, the larger the quotient, and it grows faster and faster as the gap gets near 0 (for example 24 ÷ 0.1 = 240). Accept any answer saying the number of gaps keeps growing, faster each time; reject "it grows by the same amount".
s: (a) finds 30, 40, 60 and 120, writing one as 240 ÷ a counting number
(b) finds the increases 10, 20, 60 and rejects the claim
(c) says the number of gaps keeps growing, faster and faster, as the gap shrinks

questions.q: Naina says, "When dividing by 41 there are at most 40 different non-zero remainders, so the repeating block of 1 ÷ 41 must be exactly 40 digits long." Divide 1 by 41 until a remainder returns, and say how much of her statement is right.
questions.a: Partly right. Long division gives digits 0, 2, 4, 3, 9 with remainders 10, 18, 16, 37, 1. The remainder 1 has returned, so 1 ÷ 41 = 0.0243902439... with a block of only 5 digits. The limit of 40 remainders is correct, but it is only the most that can occur, not the number that must occur.
s: carries out the division and gets remainders 10, 18, 16, 37, 1
states the repeating block is 02439, 5 digits long
says she is partly right: 40 is the greatest possible number, not the exact one

questions.q: True or False: Neel divides 9 by 40 and the first two digits after the point are both 2. He says, "Two equal digits in a row mean the quotient repeats that digit for ever, so 9 ÷ 40 = 0.222..." Give a reason.
questions.a: False. Long division gives 90 Tenths ÷ 40 = 2 with remainder 10, then 100 Hundredths ÷ 40 = 2 with remainder 20, then 200 Thousandths ÷ 40 = 5 with remainder 0, so 9 ÷ 40 = 0.225 and it ends. The remainders 10 and 20 are different, so nothing has repeated; a quotient repeats only when a remainder returns, not when a digit does.
s: states False
shows 9 ÷ 40 = 0.225 (remainders 10, 20, 0) and says repetition depends on a remainder returning, not a digit

questions.q:
A jeweller shares 4 g of silver dust equally among 27 moulds, using long division.
(a) Divide 4 by 27 until a remainder returns, listing each digit and remainder.
(b) He stops after 3 digits and puts 0.148 g in each mould. How much dust is left over? Compare it with the remainder after the 3rd digit.
(c) If he could measure to 6 digits, 0.148148 g each, would anything be left over? Explain what this shows about the division 4 ÷ 27. (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 40 Tenths ÷ 27 gives digit 1, remainder 13; 130 ÷ 27 gives digit 4, remainder 22; 220 ÷ 27 gives digit 8, remainder 4. The remainder 4 has returned, so 4 ÷ 27 = 0.148148... (b) 27 × 0.148 = 3.996 g, so 0.004 g is left: it is the remainder 4, counted in thousandths of a gram. (c) Yes: 27 × 0.148148 = 3.999996 g, so 0.000004 g is still left, the remainder 4 again, now in millionths. However far he goes, the remainder 4 keeps coming back, so the leftover gets smaller but is never 0: the division 4 ÷ 27 never ends. Accept "a tiny amount is always left because the remainder never becomes 0"; reject "nothing is left".
s: (a) lists digits 1, 4, 8 and remainders 13, 22, 4
(b) finds 0.004 g left over and links it to the remainder 4 in the thousandths place
(c) finds 0.000004 g left and explains that the remainder never becomes 0, so the division never ends

questions.q:
A page of a notebook shows two lists. Dividing 1 by 2 again and again gives 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, and dividing 1 by 5 again and again gives 0.2, 0.04, 0.008, 0.0016.
(a) Write the next number in each list.
(b) Multiply the first numbers of the lists, then the second numbers, then the third. What pattern do you see, and why does it happen?
(c) Use the fact that 16 × 625 = 10000 to write 1/16 as a decimal, and check it against the first list.
(d) Divide 1 by 24, giving each digit and remainder, until a remainder comes back. Show which remainder returns, and say what this means for whether 1 ÷ 24 ends. (1 + 1 + 1 + 2)
questions.a: (a) 0.0625 ÷ 2 = 0.03125 and 0.0016 ÷ 5 = 0.00032. (b) 0.5 × 0.2 = 0.1, 0.25 × 0.04 = 0.01 and 0.125 × 0.008 = 0.001. Each pair is 1 divided by equal numbers of 2s and 5s, and every 2 × 5 makes a 10. (c) 1/16 = 625/10000 = 0.0625, the fourth number in the first list. (d) 10 Tenths ÷ 24 gives 0, remainder 10; 100 Hundredths gives 4, remainder 4; 40 Thousandths gives 1, remainder 16; 160 gives 6, remainder 16; 160 gives 6, remainder 16 again. So 1 ÷ 24 = 0.041666... The remainder 16 has returned, so every later step is the same (digit 6, remainder 16): the remainder never becomes 0 and the division never ends.
s: (b) gets 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 and links the pattern to 2 × 5 = 10
(c) writes 625/10000 = 0.0625 and matches it to the list
(d) gets digits 0, 4, 1, 6, 6 and remainders 10, 4, 16, 16
(d) says the remainder 16 returns, so the steps repeat and the division never ends

questions.q: Hamid divides 7 by 22 and 15 by 22. He notices that both long divisions reach the remainder 18 at some step. He says, "From that step on, both divisions must give exactly the same digits, even though they started from different numbers." Carry out both divisions for five digits and judge his claim.
questions.a: Hamid is right. 7 ÷ 22: digits 3, 1, 8, 1, 8 with remainders 4, 18, 4, 18, 4, so 0.31818... 15 ÷ 22: digits 6, 8, 1, 8, 1 with remainders 18, 4, 18, 4, 18, so 0.68181... After the remainder 18, both continue 8, 1, 8, 1, ... Each next digit and remainder depends only on the remainder and the divisor (180 ÷ 22 = 8, remainder 4, every time), so once two divisions by 22 share a remainder, everything after it is the same. Accept any reason that uses the next step being fixed by the remainder and the divisor; reject agreement shown only by the digits with no reason.
s: divides 7 by 22: digits 3, 1, 8, 1, 8, remainders 4, 18, 4, 18, 4
divides 15 by 22: digits 6, 8, 1, 8, 1, remainders 18, 4, 18, 4, 18
agrees with Hamid, explaining that the next digit depends only on the remainder and the divisor

questions.q: Kunal has read that the 1000 calendar years from year 1 to year 1000 have 3,65,242 days. He says, "So every block of 1000 calendar years has 3,65,242 days, and the calendar is always 0.2 day behind the Earth." Test him on the block from year 1001 to year 2000. The Earth needs 365.2422 days for one revolution.
questions.a: He is wrong. From 1001 to 2000: 250 years are divisible by 4, 10 of them are divisible by 100, and 3 of those (1200, 1600, 2000) are divisible by 400, so there are 250 - 10 + 3 = 243 leap years (one more than the 242 from year 1 to year 1000). The block has 1000 × 365 + 243 = 3,65,243 days. The Earth needs 3,65,242.2 days, so this block is 0.8 day ahead, not 0.2 day behind.
s: counts 243 leap years, with 1200, 1600 and 2000 as the years divisible by 400
finds 3,65,243 days
compares with 3,65,242.2, finds 0.8 day ahead and rejects the claim

questions.q:
Imagine a planet that takes 90.185 of its days to go round its star. Its calendar has 90 days in a normal year and 91 in a leap year.
(a) If there were no leap years, by how many days would the calendar be behind after 100 years?
(b) Rule 1: every 5th year is a leap year. Rule 2: every 5th year is a leap year, but not every 50th year. For each rule, is the calendar ahead or behind after 100 years, and by how much?
(c) Using Rule 2, find the gap after 1000 years. Then design one more adjustment, of the kind used for the Earth's calendar, that makes the calendar match exactly over 1000 years, and check it by counting the leap years. (1 + 2 + 2)
questions.a: (a) 0.185 × 100 = 18.5 days behind. (b) The planet needs 100 × 90.185 = 9018.5 days. Rule 1 gives 20 leap years: 9000 + 20 = 9020 days, 1.5 days ahead. Rule 2 gives 20 - 2 = 18 leap years: 9018 days, 0.5 day behind. (c) In 1000 years Rule 2 gives 200 - 20 = 180 leap years: 90180 days. The planet needs 90185 days, so the calendar is 5 days behind. Adjustment: put back 5 leap years, for example every 200th year is a leap year after all. Then 5 years are divisible by 200, 20 - 5 = 15 are divisible by 50 but not by 200, and 200 - 20 = 180 are divisible by 5 but not by 50. Leap years = 180 + 5 = 185, so the days are 90000 + 185 = 90185, an exact match. Accept any rule that restores exactly 5 of the 20 skipped years in 1000 years and is checked by counting 185 leap years. Reject a rule that restores a different number of years, or one not checked by the count.
s: (a) finds 18.5 days behind
(b) finds 9020 against 9018.5 days, Rule 1 is 1.5 days ahead
(b) finds 18 leap years, 9018 days, Rule 2 is 0.5 day behind
(c) finds 90180 against 90185, 5 days behind
(c) states a rule restoring 5 leap years and checks that 185 leap years give 90185 days

questions.q: Sohan's calendar app asks two things in order. "Divisible by 100? Then 365 days." If not, "Divisible by 4? Then 366 days, otherwise 365." For which of these years does the app give the wrong number of days under today's rule?
questions.a: 2000: the app gives 365 days, because it stops at "divisible by 100" and has no step for years divisible by 400, but 2000 has 366 days. It is correct for 1900 and 2100 (365 days) and for 2024 (366 days).

questions.q:
For the years 1 to 1200, a student writes the number of leap years as 1200/4 - 1200/100 + 1200/400.
(a) Explain what each of the three terms counts, and why the second is subtracted and the third added.
(b) Find the number of days in these 1200 calendar years.
(c) Find how far the calendar is from the days the Earth takes for 1200 revolutions at 365.2422 days each, and say which is more. (1 + 1 + 1)
questions.a: (a) 1200/4 = 300 counts the years divisible by 4. 1200/100 = 12 counts the century years, which are subtracted because they lose their extra day. 1200/400 = 3 counts the years divisible by 400, which get it back. So there are 300 - 12 + 3 = 291 leap years. (b) 1200 × 365 + 291 = 438000 + 291 = 438291 days. (c) 1200 × 365.2422 = 438290.64 days, so the calendar is more, by 438291 - 438290.64 = 0.36 day.
s: (a) explains the three terms and gets 291 leap years
(b) finds 438291 days
(c) finds 438290.64 and says the calendar is more by 0.36 day
